en: A Hymn to the Ocean of Bliss (Ānandasāgarastava)
While I am far removed from the Mother of the Universe— my efforts stunted by the lack of rare opportunities to offer my petitions—
I remember the waves of her sidelong glances, which are driven forth by the wind of her genuine compassion.

Let that which is unknown be made known; or rather, let that which remains unsaid be spoken, for it is not enough merely to speak to allay internal suffering. Therefore, you are requested to lend your ear to something more than this.
O Mother, be gracious, O daughter of Malayadhvaja and Pāṇḍya! ||2||
Whether there is lamentation, weeping, or a blow to the face, whose heart would not be moved? What fruit is there in this for her,
whose mind melts and who is independent of the worlds?
O Mother, I shall speak of my distress before you.
When the mind is agitated, when speech falters,
and when the eyes whirl like a whirlpool or a pit,
who will recognize my state of being in this auspicious [moment]?
Have mercy at this time; I shall tell you right now.
May people show intense devotion toward the entire class of gods as if they were mere villagers, while toward the citizens they remain like common folk;
for, O Goddess, my heart does not turn elsewhere from your lotus feet, even though it is being dragged away.
Whether you accept this or disregard it, we shall conquer the worlds by the mere words, "We are your servants.
Indeed, O Mother of the Universe, victory is easy to achieve by this much alone.
The crowning of the heads of his servants who bear uplifted staffs. || 6 ||

"Having attained through inquiry the stainless knowledge born of the Vedānta texts, and having made it immediate through constant reflection, human beings proceed to liberation"—relying on this primordial well-spoken verse, O Daughter of the Mountain, who would be able to refute it? (7)
How many indeed are the branches of each individual Veda, and how many distinct recensions (śiras) do they have?
For some men, who are devoid of understanding the meaning, there is merely the acquisition of syllables; for them, let it be with how many more bondages of the body? (8)
The systems of logic follow mutually divergent directions, and there are thousands of such diverse supplementary treatises.
This being the case, O Daughter of the Mountain, who is capable of discerning the essential core of the meaning of these Vedic stones?
Let the method of grasping the syllables of [this] work indeed result in the understanding of its meaning for thousands of births through mere superficial exposure;
but how could one cross over the oceans of difficult prima facie arguments, thick with the waves of conceptual constructions devised by wicked disputants? (10)
"Brahmā," "Śakti," "The Liberator from Bondage," "Consisting of Māyā," "Beloved of the Destroyer of Madana"—
in merely seven or eight such shifts of terminology, [the same essence is described].
This exertion in the study of the treatise brings about capability. || 11 ||
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, you become gracious toward him who thus gradually attains direct realization;
and he whom you favor is capable of understanding this. Thus, these two exist in mutual dependence.
Listen to this discourse, having accepted it;
let someone, perhaps, understand the heart of the Śrutis.
For even for him, this [bondage] has been earned through hundreds of attachments to countless births.
May the delusion of duality vanish after some hundreds of births. || 13 ||
In this vast and boundless time, someone might perhaps attain liberation somewhere in their final birth;
such is the method of justification for the supreme scriptures.
The leading [of the meaning] to the sense of a negative particle is achieved by way of synonymous expressions.
When one person attains liberation, the entire world attains liberation;
when all have attained liberation, it is once again free from fear.
Adopting such a position as this, [one speaks].
It is not possible to abide in comfort by proceeding along a path that is not one's own. || 15 ||

O Mother, having studied the Veda, mastered the ancient scriptures, observed the various conducts of the learned, and acquired abundant wealth through teaching and other means, how could those who are indolent ever practice [virtue]? (16)
Let someone perform even laborious work; what more could he experience than that, O Mother?
He who dwells here on the border of Bhāratavarṣa lives happily, having moved just a little further north from this place.
If we were to abandon action, we would surely fall;
if we were to perform it, we would never cross over saṃsāra.
Thus, those who have set out [on the path] are caught between the injunctions: "One should abandon action" and "One should perform action."
We do not understand by what state of being these [scriptures] are called "Nigamas. || 18 ||
This is the rule for action within action: that one performs various deeds with the desire to abandon their respective consequences.
This is true; nevertheless, there will be no new bondage.
What means indeed can there be for removing this ancient bondage? || 19 ||
How much does prārabdha-karma initiate, or how much will it initiate; who indeed can determine how much this is?
For how long must I wait for time?
For whom even half a moment becomes like a hundred eons. || 20 ||
For a man who is unable to endure even half a moment of worldly existence,
the paths of Sāṅkhya and other systems do not enter his ears;
for they would require him to count all the subtle grains of sand on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
It was like the words "Eat! addressed to one afflicted by great hunger.
What indeed is devotion? If it were merely a distinction from the state of passion (*rati*), then devotion would be entirely useless because it would be a universal concomitant (*kevalānvayin*).
For who does not possess love for You, the Self of the three worlds? Indeed, there are no people in the triple world who do not harm their own selves. (22)

If it is accepted that devotion is the firm bond of affection which one extends toward You after having correctly realized that the Self is identical with all the worlds, then our desired goal is accomplished; let the object to be qualified be redundant for us, and let the qualification be superfluous. (23)

That very state which, having ascertained that [the object] is other than one's own self, finds delight through the cognition of "otherness" toward elders as if they were one's own kin—that indeed is devotion (*bhakti*).
This may be so; yet, this very [devotion] is what I must abandon.
What is greater than the delusion of duality as the root of the bondage of worldly existence? || 24 ||
Service alone is devotion; thus is the entry into the path of action.
Ritual service indeed has as its fruit the grace of the one to be served.
If it is argued that it is a stream of meditation, then by virtue of hearing [the teachings], it is the third.
O Mother, this means was already devised long ago.
Right here you shall grant me liberation; nevertheless, O Mother, I beg for my body’s fall at Maṇikarṇikā.
Let there be compassion for one's own duty—this is the nature of the Lords.
For a slave, his very state of being a laborer is likewise his own duty. || 26 ||

"O Mother, by such words from the Purāṇas as 'the acquisition of instruction comes instantly to those of virtuous deeds, but for those of sinful nature only after a great deal of time has passed,' [it is said that...]"
I am not even eager to ask for Vārāṇasī. || 27 ||
The interior is invaded by enemies such as pride and envy;
the body is pierced by wrinkles, gray hair, and hundreds of diseases;
and the home is surrounded by wives, children, and creditors.
O Mother, how may there be clarity for my mind? || 28 ||
How many in the three worlds are blessed, O Supreme Goddess, who perceive this very cycle of existence as the highest fortune,
having attained this awakening which is of the nature of a mere appearance?
"How much must I suffer on account of this worldly existence! (29)
"What kind of culture is this? What offense is its cause? And what harm has been done to you by it?"—to such questions, I am simply not skilled enough to offer a reply.
But, O Mother, I feel an indescribable sorrow that he remains in such a state.

O Mother, witness of the world, now that I have come to such a state, I lack the power even to understand what is appropriate for me here, what is the right means, how this goal is to be achieved, or what the measure is in this matter; what can I do? (31)
My own welfare is not known; I am utterly destitute of means, O Goddess, and I am incapable of observing the prescribed rules. Therefore, having no other refuge, I take refuge in you.
O Mīnākṣī, the mother of the universe and my very own mother! || 32 ||
Whatever I have smelled— something from the Vedas, something from the Āgamas, something from the Śāstras, and something from the paths of instruction—
from that, I am able to choose you.
A certain thought arose: "She shall be a protector. || 33 ||
Those who, devoid of the meaning of the scriptures, say "Brahman is thus," "I am thus," or "This is the means to attain That" are worthy of compassion as the first [type].
The second [type] are those who know only the quality of Your being the Protector.
Thus I pray for the purpose of defining the sixfold authority. || 34 ||

O Mother, as long as you possess authority over me, you may maintain your sense of "mine" toward me; what more is there to be accomplished? Why does a servant ever urge his master, saying, "Employ me in such and such a way, do not forget me"? (35)
I shall renounce what is to be renounced and perform what is prescribed; I shall act according to my capacity regarding the obligatory duties.
However, I offer this very petition to Śiva: that I may follow my intellectual and spiritual capacity rather than my physical capability for action. 36.
"The self alone is the burden"— thus, what limbs could that indolent person employ for surrender, who places that burden upon you?
For [surrender] is characterized by a distinct mark in the Witness of the universe.
This alone is the complete constituent factor for the attainment of confidence. || 37 ||
O Mother, by your instigation, there is no fault in me even for an act committed through negligence, while I am watching and breathing;
it is like a son who swallows the food given by his mother alone.
Who indeed would speak of the fault of overeating in an infant? || 38 ||
For those who seek to establish liberation through their own intellect alone,
the karma already set in motion may serve as an obstacle;
yet for those who take refuge in You alone even as their means, [it serves no such purpose].
If that were equal, O Mother, what would be the point of your boast of heroism? (39)
O Girijā, transfer or utterly destroy at its very root the *prārabdha* karma of those who have taken refuge in you;
for mortals indeed transfer the poison clinging to their own bodies to others and even cause it to be destroyed. (40)

O Goddess, having employed my senses in beholding, hearing, contemplating, and saluting You according to their respective capacities, if I were not to restrain them this very moment with a friendliness accumulated through countless births—thinking "protect me"—they would surely not remain steady. (41)
If you think, "This one must be saved," then let there be compassion for me; save me! What need have I for consideration of my good or evil deeds?
To create or to destroy the world, why this deception directed toward me, who am free from the constraints of karma? (42)
O Great Goddess, when Appayayajvan first offered his entire lineage to you by performing the rite of self-surrender (*ātmapraṇidhāna*),
who are you to neglect me, a servant of that family?
Or who else but you, my family deity, am I to worship? || 43 ||
O Mother, if out of delusion I seek refuge in another deity, what does that matter? Do I not still remain his own?
Would a beast belonging to the king, by entering another's house through ignorance, thereby become the property of that other? || 44 ||
O fools, having placed this great burden upon your heads in vain, how is it that you sink into this ocean of existence? Having instead cast the entire burden at the feet of your Mother!
Confidently [cross] this [ocean], which is like a mere puddle, from the north. || 45 ||
"Where will this body fall? Where must one go after that? Who will punish it, or for how long a time?
What is the means for its crossing over?"—thus [the thoughts] are endless.
The anxiety that had been fixed upon you has now been gradually laid to rest.
"Should I seek knowledge, or should I uplift [the soul] even without it? Should I conceal my past actions (*prārabdha*),
or should I restrain them?"— thus [is the thought] of her who is entirely subject to the single act of taking refuge (*sakṛt-prapadana*).
A great anxiety arose in my mother regarding me here. || 47 ||
This is the discernment between the insentient and the sentient,
and this alone is the skill in purifying the principles beginning with earth;
and this is the Śaiva knowledge obtainable through millions of scriptures.
Since my very self has been placed at the pair of feet of my mother. || 48 ||
My self has been placed by me at your feet, O beloved of the Lord of Hālāsya, which dwell amidst the thirty-six coverings (āvaraṇas).
Who among those existing on earth, in the netherworld, or in the heavens would be able to endure [the weight of it]?
That eye and the others [of yours] are unable to behold me with a steady gaze. || 49 ||
"O Mother, it is certain that you will remove my bondage and bestow happiness; all of that already exists.
Now, having entrusted my entire burden to you,"
Why should I choose even this over my own liberation? || 50 ||
Cast your body into the Kāśī river, or into the home of a dog-cooker;
lead me to heaven, or to liberation, or to a downward rebirth;
show mercy this very day, or at some time in the future.
What anxiety do I have regarding wealth? The wealthy man is the authority [in this matter]. || 51 ||
I cannot endure an interruption in hearing your stories, nor can I endure even a moment’s lapse in the worship of your feet.
Grant me liberation; this [desire] is not inconsistent with that goal. O Mother, let there be no great obstacle to my final emancipation.

O Mother, constantly remembering from head to foot each limb of yours—the auspiciousness of the world—I am tossed by the successive waves of the ocean of bliss; thus, I do not take note of the days that pass.

O Mother, may I remember this foot of yours—which, though as hard as stone, appears pale-red on my head as if from the pressure of circumambulation—and which is as tender as fresh butter churned from the ocean of nectar. 54.
O Mother, whatever few teachers there may be in the three worlds, even they have attained their status as teachers only by having you yourself approach them;
for we cross this ocean of saṃsāra with ease simply by having you hold us by the foot upon our heads.
In the conquest of Smara, which is accomplished by the lady with the tilaka-marked eyes,
Śiva may indeed share the entire glory;
but when it was achieved by you, O Mother, through the mere employment of your left foot alone— [how much more so]!
Or what possibility is there even for the Lord of the Past (Śiva) to be subject to the conquest of time? || 56 ||
O Mother of the Universe, if my mind were tender, let there be a sandal for Your two soft feet;
if it were harsh, [let there be one] for grasping the hand of the Enemy of Tripura.
May there be utility for you in the ritual of placing the stone upon the head. || 57 ||
Since your lotus-heart is firmly attached here to the surface of your feet, which possess a most glossy and charming luster,
this very line upon your foot is the one that indicates your imperial sovereignty over the two hundred and one worlds.

O Mother, O Madhureśvarī, forgive this childish act of mine, who am terrified of sinking into the ocean of worldly existence, that I grasped your feet so firmly, disregarding their extraordinary tenderness.

O Mother, how is it that harsh words do not pierce my feet, even though they were once crushed during the offering of flowers— those very feet upon which Paśupati, when offended by a lapse in affection, would touch with the tip of the crescent moon only very gently?

O Compassionate One, even if You were to reveal but once Your lotus feet—which are naturally beautiful, unsurpassed, immeasurable, extraordinary, and supremely auspicious—by what eye indeed shall I behold them? 61.
Even divine eyes are indeed capable of discerning those objects worthy of being grasped by the denizens of heaven; yet,
regarding your embodied form, whose majesty is perceivable only by you, [they are not so].
Only devotion to you remains as our refuge.
In this vast and indeed limitless wheel of time,
blessed are those few, such as the eminent Śuka-yogi,
who, possessing perfectly pure beings, have dissolved themselves into the pair of your feet.
We recognize those as being your own nails.
O Mother, this moon, who has been cherished by you with a sense of "mine-ness" since childhood, now desires to discharge its debt to you;
it surely divides itself into many parts and places them at your feet under the guise of its rays.
I have heard nothing that has entered within me, being obstructed by the rock of atheistic doctrine;
therefore, I shall cast this great rock down below with a mere drop of water from the feet of the Supreme Deity.
May I indeed hear her voice at the time of her departure, as she comes of her own accord out of compassion for me, her child, while I am being surrounded by the armored soldiers of Yama.
O Mother, [I am captivated by] the tinkling sounds of the jeweled anklets on your feet.
O Mother, when will you grant me your lap, which has been occupied and released in turn by many youths headed by Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava?
They say, indeed, that a son who is dear to his mother is dull-witted. || 67 ||

Having placed my head upon the thigh of the Lord—my fatigue dispelled by the breeze from the sprout-like hem of his robe offered out of compassion—might I, even in this very life, hear the supreme instruction here in Maṇikarṇikā? (68)

O Mother, I meditate upon your expansive orb of hips, which adorns the couch of the Enemy of Tripura; it shines with the splendor of its lower portion, where golden garments are visible, fastened by the thread of your girdle. 69.

Having placed even the fourteen worlds within her womb, you, with a resolute mind, have surely fashioned a golden, thick bandage as a rampart all around them for their protection; this is my conjecture.

Moreover, even if the liberated souls in Tripura do not abandon the slope of your breasts out of a longing for your milk, for what reason would they not moisten our faces, which are scorched by the fierce fever of worldly existence? 71.
Having finally regained the child who was long lost,
the pearl necklace of the Supreme Goddess— her heart overwhelmed with maternal affection—
shines like a continuous stream of milk-drops flowing from her swelling breasts.
O Goddess, may that sugarcane bow made of the minds of men have my heart as its base;
for it is said that during the rite of stringing the bow, it might perhaps be stepped upon by the hem of Your garment.

O Mother, having assumed some most cruel disposition in order to discipline even those who have committed the gravest of sins, you take these flowers in place of arrows; indeed, such harshness toward your own children is truly excessive!
Visualizing the noose and the goad in Your hands,
they paralyze and bring all worlds under their control;
O Mother, by remembering Your bow and arrow even once, [they achieve the same].
Having descended onto the path of enjoyment, they assume the state of kings. || 75 ||
Fortunate indeed are those who know the ultimate truth; contemplating the noose and the goad in your hand, they conquer passion and hatred.
Perceiving the bow on one side and the arrow on the other, they turn their hearts away from the dark well of sense objects.
"O Śrutis, you say that this internal refuge of people, the moon, departs [at death] and enters [the sun];
let this be so. But as for me, O Goddess, my mind has now firmly dissolved into your moon-like face. (77)
O Mother of the Self of Knowledge, who is capable of describing such stainless purity of your row of teeth,
from which this pure progenitor of words has arisen?
The fame of the poet, which is rooted in that [work], is therefore all the greater. || 78 ||
For although your row of teeth is indeed clear, it bears the beauty of pomegranate seeds crushed at will;
therefore, against its deep crimson hue intensified by the mingling of dust, [the pearls on your lip appear as if they were mere specks].
I think that it is through supreme familiarity with the mind. || 79 ||
O Mother, if half of Your smile has already conquered the Triple City, then the other half must likewise do so;
O Mother, I contemplate that smile of Yours as being for the sake of pacifying the Tripura composed of the causal, subtle, and gross forms.

May the gentle smile of my mother—which resembles fresh butter churned from within the vessel of her own agitation upon seeing my afflictions, and which dispels the inner darkness of those people who remember it—be for the welfare and auspiciousness of the world. 81.

O Mother, place within the bud of my mouth that essence of betel, which is the condensed divine fragrance of the lotuses of the eternal forest, perfumed by the crescent moon, and the very essence of the understanding of all the scriptures. 82.
O Śivā, because of our long-standing intimacy, the jewel upon your nose does not appear to the minds of those whose wealth is their asceticism;
it shines only to signal the end of the night of the continuous succession of ignorance.
She appeared like the pupil in the eye of the Teacher of the Asuras.
Under the guise of the reflections of the pearl-ornaments in your earrings, which are clearly visible upon cheeks blooming with the filling of betel,
the orb of your face bears within its interior that primordial color, pure and stainless, resulting from the union of the two suns.
O Mother, such is your glance— bestowing manifold prosperity, granting auspiciousness, and bestowing even the station of the Lord of the Gods with ease— or perhaps it is even greater than this.
Even now, she is not able to pass beyond my ear. 85.

This moonlight of your eyes has entered the vast forest of the Upaniṣads, which is as hard as a mass of stone, difficult for people to penetrate, and where its presence is futile; by whom could it be served? Cast it upon me once, while I am suffering! 86.
"O Mother, is this praise of you: 'By your glance, that which was quelled by Śiva has been vomited up again'?
For her, who brings forth the four aims of human life as a mere play, that statement is rather a figurative expression (avayutyavāda). (87)
Noble ones, you should not be deluded into thinking that when the Veda declares Soma to be the progenitor of the world, this refers merely to the creeper.
This teaching is concerned with that Moon who, as the very self of your vision, abiding within the Śaiva and Vāma systems, creates the universe. 88.
O Mother, since your gaze, which is so generous in giving, perceives the earth as the point of a needle and Mount Meru as an atom,
we too have been seen by you here; therefore, we remember [you].
[He crossed] that very ocean of existence, which is like a lake with surging waves. || 89 ||
O Mother, your sidelong glances— white as camphor by virtue of being the abode of speech, possessing the luster of the filaments of white water-lilies through their association with lotuses,
and turned dark by the power of cleansing the mental impurity of those who seek refuge— triumph!
O Mother, this line drawn with black collyrium, shimmering at the corner of your eye up to your ear,
shines like a row of moss that has formed a continuous connection following the path of a surging flood of compassion.
How can that glance, which creates and destroys the universe, be of a fickle nature?
For even this [glance] gains glory only by following her;
O Goddess, I place my trust in that very compassion of yours.
"One half of Śambhu is compassion itself, free from all blemish; the other half consists of all other qualities combined together.
O Mother, this secret has now indeed flashed forth for me as I behold that half of Īśvara which is composed of you.
O Mother, for the sake of directing each deity to his own specific task, the gods have stationed themselves silently at the base of your eyebrows, watching your movements with undivided attention.
The gaze attains the state of being a musk-paste tilaka mark. || 94 ||

This orb of your face, O Goddess, was fashioned by gathering the very essence—drop by drop—from the thousand rays of the sun; meanwhile, the entire multitude of the moon’s dark spots were later deposited together in the guise of your hair.
This fragment of the moon, as pure as crystal, placed upon your hair which is as beautiful as a cluster of Indra’s jewels,
assumes the appearance of a blue-lotus petal ornament due to its contact with that dark support.
O Sovereign of the Three Worlds, the Cintāmaṇi and the Kaustubha are renowned as the two jewels situated upon the paved courtyard of your palace;
what other jewel could there be that would surpass even the crest of your crown?
Let Vācaspati and the others describe you. || 97 ||
Some remember, in their final birth, those waves which were as red as hundreds of rising suns, as cool as ten thousand full moons, and composed of the flowing essence of the sentiment of love. 98.
May that indescribable Being manifest before me— He whose body is anointed with a thick paste of intense saffron, who is beautiful with a multitude of jeweled ornaments set upon every limb,
whose mouth is filled with betel, who bears the young moon as His crest,
and who is entirely crimson.

O Goddess, you have assumed this body possessing the characteristics of both female and male in order to demonstrate that in this triple world of moving and unmoving beings, half consists of women and half of men; therefore, you are known as one whose very body is the three worlds.
O Girijā, Maheśa creates, withdraws, and sustains the three worlds; does he even know this fact?
It is only through your companionship with that Lord that the doctrine of his being the progenitor of the universe has arisen even in the Vedas. (101)
You are the consciousness of existence, the fragmentary bliss that is indifferent even toward the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds.
To say that "Śiva remains" apart from you is the talk of one who lacks true knowledge; for what half of Śiva could there be without you? 102.
The sun does not scorch here, nor does the wind blow;
the entire world does not even know its activity.
Such is this inner apartment of the Lord of Death, where fools like us move about in comfort.
May there be no land for me devoid of Your presence; may there be no learning for me devoid of the knowledge of Your true nature;
may there be no lineage for me devoid of devotion to Your feet; and may there be no life for me devoid of meditation upon You. (104)
O Goddess, who is capable even of speaking or understanding what you are like, or that you are exactly as you appear?
O Mother, being utterly ignorant even of myself, this most vulgar man feels ashamed to offer praise unto you.
Whether this work has been completed or not, and whether it has been offered to you or not— no spark of joy arises within my inner being;
for whatever ignorance is evident here, that belongs to me alone.
But, O Mother, I place my trust in you as the refuge of the wretched. || 106 ||
O Mother, disregarding the times of the solstices, equinoxes, and transits, even when the moon and the sun have both set,
may I remember your lotus-feet, which are characterized by bliss and in which all duality has been cast away.

I worship the form of the Mother of the World, which takes the shape of the *Caturadhyāyī*, whose insignia is the *kalahaṃsa* bird, whose body consists of the Supreme Brahman, and which is adorned within by the crescent moon. 108.
Thus ends the Śrī Ānandasāgarastava composed by Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita.
